description: We are a team of data detectives using NASA's Earth observations to uncover how our environment in Pakistan is changing, and to prove whether those changes are real.
summary: Hot Nights, Hidden Risk measures how land surface temperature changed in Rawalpindi-Islamabad over 20 years (2003-2022) using NASA MODIS Aqua MYD11A2 data (1 km, 8-day, day and night) from NASA AppEEARS. We kept good-quality pixels, averaged each zone by year, and tested trends with Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test. We also tested whether the city pulled away from nearby farmland by testing the city-minus-rural gap directly, and mapped the trend for every 1 km pixel. Result: urban nights warmed +0.77 °C per decade (p < 0.001) against +0.39 in farmland, so the night gap widened by +0.41 °C per decade (p < 0.001). Daytime urban change was not significant (+0.18 °C per decade, p = 0.586). A stricter quality-filter check confirms the night result; the daytime gap could not be re-tested. This matters because hot nights deny people recovery, raise electricity demand for cooling, and hit people without air conditioning hardest. The code, results and 7-slide demo are public. AI tools (DeepSeek and Claude) helped write the code.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: The project turns 20 years of NASA satellite land surface temperature into a plain-language urban heat assessment for Rawalpindi-Islamabad. It reports separate day and night trends for the built-up core and two farmland reference zones, tests whether the city-rural gap changed, and maps where the strongest pixel-level trends occur.
HOW IT WORKS:

(1) We requested MYD11A2.061 (MODIS Aqua, 8-day, 1 km) through NASA AppEEARS for 2003-2022 with LST_Day_1km, LST_Night_1km, QC_Day and QC_Night.

(2) We kept good-quality pixels, applied the same quality rule to every zone and to day and night, and averaged each zone by year to remove the seasonal cycle.

(3) We estimated trends with Sen's slope and tested them with the Mann-Kendall test at p < 0.05.

(4) We tested the city-minus-rural gap directly, and only call the city "faster warming" if that test is significant.

(5) We repeated the test for every 1 km pixel to produce day and night trend maps.

RESULT: Over 2003-2022 the urban core warmed by +0.77 °C per decade at night (p < 0.001) against +0.39 in farmland, so the night gap widened by +0.41 °C per decade (p < 0.001). Daytime urban change was not significant (+0.18 °C per decade, p = 0.586). A stricter quality-filter check confirms the night result, but the urban daytime series then has too few usable years to re-test the daytime gap.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: Hot nights reduce the body's chance to recover, raise cooling demand and electricity use, and hit people without air conditioning hardest. A trend with an honest significance test is more useful to planners than a dramatic number without one.

TOOLS: Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Matplotlib), Streamlit and Plotly, Google Colab, GitHub, NASA AppEEARS and MODIS MYD11A2.061. AI tools (DeepSeek and Claude) helped draft and debug the code. The team chose the question, data and zones, ran the code on real NASA data, checked the numbers and wrote the conclusions.

LIMITS: This is surface temperature, not air temperature. Rural zones are hand-drawn boxes, 1 km pixels smooth over streets and parks, and about 1 in 20 tests can be a false positive.
dataRefs: MODIS Aqua MYD11A2.061 Land Surface Temperature
